cues.text: In the small village of Cimballa , in the province of Zaragoza in the Kingdom of Aragon, the parish priest was known as Don Tommaso.
For many months, he had been quietly troubled by doubt concerning the true presence of Christ in the Eucharist, a struggle he kept to himself even as he continued to celebrate Mass.
Flesh and Blood at the Consecration
On the Feast of the Purification, February 2, 1370, as Don Tommaso pronounced the words of consecration during Mass, the Host is said to have transformed visibly into flesh.
Blood flowed from it, staining the altar linen beneath — a sign that struck directly at the doubt he had carried in silence for so long.
The sign did more than resolve an intellectual doubt.
Don Tommaso resigned his parish altogether not long afterward and retired to a monastery, choosing penance and prayer over ordinary ministry for the remainder of his life.
The Bishop of Zaragoza, Pedro Pérez Calvillo , placed the miraculous Host and blood-stained altar cloth in the tabernacle for the village's veneration.
The relic was later moved to Zaragoza's Royal Chapel of the Aljafería Palace during ongoing war between Aragon and Castile, for its greater safety.
The village of Cimballa has called the episode their Most Holy Doubtful Mystery ever since.
It keeps the anniversary each year on September 12, when the blood-stained corporal relic is still venerated in the parish church of the Purification of Our Lady.
A priest's private, months-long crisis of faith remains, in the memory the village has kept, not a private failure to be hidden but the very occasion of the sign that resolved it.
